parts: A famous menu says that on Christmas Day, eighteen seventy, a Paris restaurant offered elephant soup.
The menu also lists roast camel.
And a cat, surrounded by rats.
It sounds like a joke.
The hunger behind it was not.
People say all Paris dined on the zoo, and that is only half true.
Did Paris really eat the zoo?
And if so, who got to eat it?
We will mark each claim: documented, disputed, myth, or no evidence found.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
First, the siege.
On September nineteenth, eighteen seventy, the Prussian army closed the ring around Paris.
An armistice came on January twenty-eighth.
That is more than four months.
Victor Hugo kept notes through all of it.
In late October he wrote: we eat horse in every form.
Two other diarists tell the same story.
Edmond de Goncourt was a French novelist.
Henry Labouchère was an English journalist trapped in the city.
In October, Labouchère reported a meat ration of one hundred grams, and queues of about two hours.
By mid-November, he wrote, it was thirty grams a head.
In almost every district.
That is about one ounce.
In January, Goncourt reported straw in the bread.
Labouchère called it dark, heavy, and gritty.
He put the bread ration at three hundred grams for adults, and half that for children.
Hugo said his own hens refused the black bread.
A modern study of one poor district found that deaths more than doubled during the siege and the Commune that followed.
So on hunger, the record is clear.
Documented.
Now, what was on the plate?
Horse came first, then donkey and mule.
In October, Goncourt wrote that horse meat was slyly creeping into Parisian cooking.
Labouchère tried donkey and found it firm and savory.
In December, he noted a butcher who sold dogs, cats, and rats.
Customers looked around before they went in.
Rats had a price too.
Between forty centimes and a franc and a half, depending on the diarist.
On December thirtieth, Hugo wrote: we are eating the unknown.
How many people ate them?
We found no count.
So dogs, cats, and rats on a plate: documented.
And then the zoo.
The Jardin d'Acclimatation was a garden of exotic animals.
Its official website says it was forced to sacrifice its animals to feed the starving population.
On December fifth, Labouchère wrote that almost all the animals of the Acclimatation garden had been eaten.
They averaged about seven francs a pound.
Kangaroo sold for twelve.
The city of Paris says the garden's animals went to the highest bidder.
So the zoo did end up on plates.
Documented.
Now the stars of the story: two elephants, Castor and Pollux.
Goncourt saw a butcher's shop on the Boulevard Haussmann.
On December thirty-first, he saw the trunk of young Pollux for sale.
The butcher said forty francs a pound.
That same day he found the famous elephant sausage at the restaurant Voisin.
On January fifth, Labouchère ate a slice of Pollux.
It was tough, coarse, and oily, he wrote.
He did not recommend it to English families.
He put the trunks at forty-five francs a pound.
Hugo wrote on January twelfth: we ate an elephant steak this morning.
So elephant on a Paris plate: documented.
But here the story gets tangled.
Which garden did they live in?
Goncourt says the Acclimatation garden.
Hugo mentions an elephant of the Jardin des Plantes.
Even modern sources split.
The Acclimatation garden itself says they were theirs.
The city of Paris says the garden's animals were moved to the Jardin des Plantes.
When did they die?
Modern sources give dates from late November to the end of December.
Goncourt proves only that Pollux was dead by December thirty-first.
So now, the famous Christmas card.
A printed menu from the restaurant Voisin is dated December twenty-fifth.
It says day ninety-nine of the siege.
It lists elephant consommé, roast camel, and cat flanked by rats.
We read those words in a guidebook from nineteen eleven.
The guide says favored diners were handed a pink souvenir card.
Some of those dates would make that soup impossible.
Here are three ideas.
Maybe the date on the card is wrong.
Maybe Voisin used a different elephant.
Maybe the card is a later souvenir.
We could not find an original in a museum collection.
So the Christmas soup is disputed.
Was it propaganda?
Was the zoo menu a message of defiance?
Proof would look like an order, a poster, or a newspaper campaign.
In the sources we could open, we found none.
But we could not open the French newspaper archives.
So that is a gap in our search, not a verdict.
Goncourt noted that restaurant menus offered buffalo, antelope, and kangaroo, all authentic.
Our reading: for the restaurants, this was business and theater.
A strange dish fills a table.
Propaganda: no evidence found.
Now the question that matters most: who could pay?
A National Guard soldier was paid thirty sous a day.
A sou is a twentieth of a franc.
So that is a franc and a half.
Remember the trunk: forty francs a pound.
That is about twenty-seven days of that pay, for one pound.
Labouchère says the other cuts cost about ten francs a pound.
Almost a week of pay.
In December he listed a turkey at sixty francs.
Forty days of pay.
In mid-January, Hugo noted an egg at two francs seventy-five.
Almost two days of pay, for one egg.
Those sums are our own calculation.
Hugo received antelope, bear, and deer as gifts.
Labouchère wrote that in fashionable restaurants the supply was unlimited, and so was the price.
Goncourt heard of a well-dressed woman asking a butcher for a sou's worth of horse scrapings.
Our reading: hunger crossed classes. The choice of meat did not.
Labouchère wrote that the wives and children of guardsmen went to canteens for soup.
So did Paris eat the zoo?
Not all of Paris.
The zoo went to those who could pay, or who had friends.
The idea that all Paris dined on the zoo: myth.
The zoo was for those who could pay: documented.
Now let us count the evidence.
Hunger was real: documented.
Dogs, cats, and rats were eaten: documented.
Elephant was sold and eaten: documented.
The Christmas card with elephant soup: disputed.
Which garden they belonged to: disputed.
An official propaganda campaign: no evidence found.
All of Paris dining on the zoo: myth.
The surprise is how unequal the plates were.
Our reading: the zoo story survives because it is strange.
Horse and brown bread are forgotten because they are ordinary.
Behind every strange menu was an ordinary hunger.
So what is still open?
One: when exactly did Castor and Pollux die?
Two: was the Christmas card printed that day, or later?
Three: how many people ate dogs, cats, and rats?
Four: did anyone in authority encourage the zoo menus?
The French newspapers of that winter may hold answers.
A dated original card, or a newspaper from that morning, could settle the second one.
Our reading: necessity for most, spectacle for a few.
One more detail.
Many of Labouchère's letters left Paris by balloon.
The Acclimatation garden also housed carrier pigeons.
A city cut off from the world still found ways to send news.
So here is a last question.
Another dinner story everyone knows: did the Romans have a room for vomiting?
